metadata.scope: e_guinea (295 baronies across k_akan, k_borgu, k_guinea, k_gur, k_igbo-benue, k_kong, k_yorubaland)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding (stripped of key prefixes and parenthetical notes).
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier extracted from modern_name; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.anachronism_type: Mutually exclusive historicity category: attested_pre_867 | fictional_placeholder | post_867_eponym | renamed_post_867 | modern_anachronism | early_modern_foundation | high_late_medieval_attestation | unattested_indigenous_or_minor.
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= that bookmark year.
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation for the audited name (negative values = BCE; null if unattested).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.eponym: Structured eponym object {year, post_867, type, details} when named after a person, saint, ruler, deity, or dynasty/tribe; null otherwise.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.historical_names: List of distinct pre-867 attested names for the same site or immediate predecessor: [{name, native_script, language, attested_from, attested_to, source, relationship, notes}].
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_aowin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Akan Kingdom of Aowin (also known as Ebrosa) is documented in 17th- and early 18th-century regional and European accounts (e.g., Denkyira wars c. 1680–1696 CE and Asante conquest in 1715 CE).

morphemes.translation: ethnonym and historical kingdom name in southwestern Ghana

b_aowin.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Akan/Anyi ethnonym and polity name for the southwestern forest kingdom between the Tano and Bia rivers; also historically referred to as Ebrosa.

b_sanwi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; established c. 1740 CE in oral tradition by Anyi migrants from Aowin with its capital at Krindjabo, and documented in the 1843 CE French protectorate treaty.

morphemes.translation: traditional Anyi kingdom name in southeastern Ivory Coast

b_sanwi.etymology_analysis: Anyi polity and territorial name derived from the successor state founded by Aowin migrants in southeastern Ivory Coast.

b_sehwi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kingdom of Sefwi (Sehwi) emerged in the 17th century CE and appears in 18th- and 19th-century European records (e.g., Bowdich 1819 CE).

morphemes.translation: ethnonym and kingdom name (traditionally glossed as 'war is over')

b_sehwi.etymology_analysis: Akan/Bia ethnonym and polity name (also spelled Sefwi), traditionally explained in oral history as signifying a place of refuge where war had ended.

b_attie.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Attié (Akyé) history prior to French colonial administration in the late 19th century CE is preserved primarily through oral tradition.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym of the Attié (Akyé) people of southeastern Ivory Coast

b_attie.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Kwa-speaking Attié (Akyé) people inhabiting the forest zone north of Abidjan in southeastern Ivory Coast.

b_east_attie.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern/in-game directional subdivision of Attié territory.
b_east_attie.etymology_analysis: English cardinal-direction qualifier prefixed to the Kwa ethnonym Attié.

b_north_attie.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern/in-game directional subdivision of Attié territory.
b_north_attie.etymology_analysis: English cardinal-direction qualifier prefixed to the Kwa ethnonym Attié.

b_west_attie.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern/in-game directional subdivision of Attié territory.
b_west_attie.etymology_analysis: English cardinal-direction qualifier prefixed to the Kwa ethnonym Attié.

b_dabou.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Dabou is documented in French colonial-era records in southern Ivory Coast.
b_dabou.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Kwa (Adjoukrou) settlement toponym on the north shore of Ébrié Lagoon in southern Ivory Coast.

b_tiagba.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tiagba is a stilt-built lagoon village on Ébrié Lagoon without pre-867 documentary records.
b_tiagba.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Ahizi/Kwa toponym for the stilt village on the north shore of Ébrié Lagoon in southern Ivory Coast.

b_adanse_manso.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; although archaeological radiocarbon dates at Adansemanso indicate occupation from c. 393 CE and 9th-century CE development, written/documentary records of Adanse begin in the 16th–17th centuries CE.
b_adanse_manso.etymology_analysis: Akan compound meaning 'capital/seat of Adanse', where Adanse derives from Twi adanseɛ ('builders'), commemorating the construction of permanent houses and shrines.

b_adaboye.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Adaboye (Adaboye Abuakwa) appears in Asona clan oral traditions of Adanse recorded in the modern era.

morphemes.translation: ancestral Asona clan settlement name in Adanse

b_adaboye.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Akan settlement name in Adanse associated in oral tradition with the early Asona matriclan.

b_assin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Akan kingdom of Assin (Asen) rose during the 16th and 17th centuries CE as part of the inland Akani trade network.
b_assin.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Akan ethnonym and polity name (Asen/Assin) in central Ghana.

b_elmina.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; documented history of Elmina begins in 1482 CE with the Portuguese agreement between Diogo de Azambuja and the local ruler to build São Jorge da Mina.

morphemes.translation: mine (referring to the Gold Coast gold trade)

b_elmina.etymology_analysis: European-derived exonym from Portuguese A Mina ('the mine'), referring to the coastal gold trade around São Jorge da Mina (known locally in Fante as Edina).

b_mankessim.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mankessim is documented in 17th-century CE European accounts (such as Dapper and Bosman) as the capital of Fante.
b_mankessim.etymology_analysis: Fante compound meaning 'within the great state/town', reflecting Mankessim's role as the traditional sacred and political headquarters of the Fante.

b_shama.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Shama (locally Esima) enters written records in the 16th century CE with Portuguese coastal trade and Fort St. Sebastian.
b_shama.etymology_analysis: Coastal Ahanta/Akan settlement name at the mouth of the Pra River, recorded by European traders in the 16th century.

b_kumasi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; founded in the 1680s CE per Asante oral tradition under Osei Kofi Tutu I and documented in early 19th-century European accounts (e.g., Bowdich 1819 CE).
b_kumasi.etymology_analysis: Twi compound meaning 'under the kum tree', commemorating the site where Osei Tutu or Okomfo Anokye established the Asante capital in the 1680s.

b_asante_manso.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; although excavations show occupation from the 1st millennium BCE and 9th-century CE activity, there is no written attestation <= 867 CE and the ethnonym 'Asante' dates to the 17th century CE.
b_asante_manso.etymology_analysis: Twi compound combining Asante (from ɔsa nti, 'because of war') and manso ('seat of the state'), denoting the sacred ancestral cradle of the Oyoko and Aduana clans.

b_bekwai.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; settled by the Oyoko clan as part of the early Asante nucleus in the 17th century CE.

morphemes.translation: Asante town and traditional state name

b_bekwai.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Asante Twi toponym (Bɛkwae) for one of the core Oyoko towns south of Kumasi.

b_manso_nkwanta.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern district capital in Amansie West with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_manso_nkwanta.etymology_analysis: Akan compound combining the territorial/settlement name Manso with Twi nkwanta ('crossroads').

b_kwahu-south.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kwahu (Kwawu) appears in 17th-century CE European records, and Kwahu South District was created in 1988 CE.
b_kwahu-south.etymology_analysis: Combines Kwahu (traditionally derived from Twi akoa wu, 'the slave died') with the modern English administrative qualifier South.

b_bukuruwa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bukuruwa appears in Kwahu oral migration traditions and early 20th-century colonial records (e.g., Perregaux 1903 CE).
b_bukuruwa.etymology_analysis: Akan (Kwahu Twi) settlement name meaning 'stone jar'.

b_shai.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Shai (Sɛ) is documented in post-15th-century European coastal and Accra Plains records.

morphemes.translation: Dangme subgroup and hill area name (Sɛ)

b_shai.etymology_analysis: Anglicized rendering of Sɛ, the Ga-Dangme ethnonym and territorial name associated with the Shai Hills north of Accra.

b_accra.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Accra enters written history in 16th- and 17th-century CE European coastal trade records.

morphemes.translation: driver/soldier ants (referring to anthills in the area)

b_accra.etymology_analysis: European adaptation of the Akan (Twi) name Nkran ('soldier ants'), applied by Twi speakers to the Ga coastal settlement and its surrounding anthill-dotted plains.

b_tarkwa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tarkwa developed as a Wassa Fiase gold-mining town documented in the 19th century CE.

morphemes.translation: traditionally glossed as 'my bed' or 'my resting place'

b_tarkwa.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Nzema/Wassa toponym in the Western Region of Ghana, traditionally explained as 'my bed' or 'resting place'.

b_beyin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the coast around Beyin was named Apollonia by Portuguese explorers and hosted European trading posts from 1655 CE (Fort Apollonia).
b_beyin.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Nzema toponym for the traditional capital of Western Nzema on the Gulf of Guinea.

b_wassa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Wassa (Wasa) polity is documented in post-15th-century European Gold Coast trade records.

morphemes.translation: ethnonym and traditional Akan territory name

b_wassa.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Akan ethnonym and territorial designation for the gold-rich Wassa Traditional Area in southwestern Ghana.

b_begho.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Begho (also known as Nsoko, Bighu, or Bitu) flourished from the 15th to 18th centuries CE and appears in early modern Mande and European sources.

morphemes.translation: historical market city name (also known as Nsoko or Bitu)

b_begho.etymology_analysis: Historical name of the major Bono/Mande commercial town near Hani on the forest-savanna transition zone.

b_banda.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Banda (Banda Ahenkro) is documented in post-medieval Bono and Gyaman regional history.
b_banda.etymology_analysis: Regional ethnonym and settlement name in northwestern Bono, Ghana.

b_sampa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sampa is a modern district capital (Jaman North) in the Bono Region with no pre-867 written record.
b_sampa.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Nafaanra/Bono settlement name on the Ghana–Ivory Coast border.

b_wenchi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; although nearby Bonoso has radiocarbon dates of 663–774 CE, written records of Wenchi (Wankyi) date to the post-medieval/colonial era.

morphemes.translation: aardvark (totemic animal; alternatively waan akyi, 'beyond brightness')

b_wenchi.etymology_analysis: Anglicized spelling of Wankyi, traditionally derived either from wankyie (the aardvark that unearthed the ancestors) or waan akyi ('beyond brightness').

b_bono_manso.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; founded archaeologically c. 1000 CE, and first attested in European cartography as 'Bonnoe' on a 1629 CE Dutch map.
b_bono_manso.etymology_analysis: Bono Twi compound meaning 'seat of the Bono state', where Bono means 'pioneer/first-born' (abɔnɔwo) or refers to the ancestral rock shelter (boɔ) at Amowi.

b_kintampo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; while the prehistoric Kintampo Complex is named after the town, written records of Kintampo itself date to the 19th century CE.
b_kintampo.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Bono Twi settlement name on the savanna-forest trade corridor, traditionally explained as 'cattle crossing'.

b_prang.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Prang is a modern district capital (Pru West) in Ghana's Bono East Region without pre-867 documentary records.
b_prang.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Guan/Bono settlement toponym in the Pru river basin of central Ghana.

b_ahwene_koko.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; excavations at Ahwene Koko yielded a date of c. 1585 CE, and it is known from 17th-century Wenchi oral history.
b_ahwene_koko.etymology_analysis: Akan Twi compound meaning 'red beads', the name of the 17th-century capital of Wenchi.

b_upper_tano.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Tano River (Ta Kora) is documented in post-medieval Akan oral tradition and 19th-century European accounts (e.g., Bowdich 1819 CE).

morphemes.translation: sacred river and deity Ta Kora

b_upper_tano.etymology_analysis: English geographic qualifier ('Upper') combined with the indigenous Akan hydronym Tano, personified in Bono religion as the supreme abosom Ta Kora.

b_tekyiman.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Techiman (Takyiman) succeeded Bono Manso as the Bono capital after 1723 CE.
b_tekyiman.etymology_analysis: Bono Twi compound (Takyiman) combining the traditional founder's name Takyi with ɔman ('state/nation').

b_middle_tano.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Tano River (Ta Kora) is documented in post-medieval Akan oral tradition and 19th-century European accounts (e.g., Bowdich 1819 CE).

morphemes.translation: sacred river and deity Ta Kora

b_middle_tano.etymology_analysis: English geographic qualifier ('Middle') combined with the indigenous Akan hydronym Tano.

b_atebubu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Atebubu was a traditional Guan-Bono kingdom documented in the colonial era.

morphemes.translation: traditional Guan-Bono kingdom and town name

b_atebubu.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Guan/Bono polity and town name in the Bono East Region of Ghana.

b_donkoro_nkwanta.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Donkoro Nkwanta is an old Bono town on the Kumasi–Kintampo road without pre-867 documentary records.
b_donkoro_nkwanta.etymology_analysis: Bono Twi compound combining Donkoro with nkwanta ('crossroads'), reflecting its position along the Kumasi–Kintampo route.

b_mampon.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Asante Mampong became a major Bretuo clan stool within the Asante confederacy in the late 17th century CE.
b_mampon.etymology_analysis: Akan Twi compound from ɔman ('state/town') and pɔn ('great/large'), meaning 'great state/town'.

b_ganeboafo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ganeboafo is cited in secondary/oral accounts as a Guan settlement on the Afram Plains c. 1200 CE.

morphemes.translation: historical Guan settlement name on the Afram Plains

b_ganeboafo.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Guan/Akan settlement name associated with medieval Guan occupation of the Afram Plains.

b_bassa-afram.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bassa is a traditional area in Sene/Afram Plains documented in modern Ghanaian administrative records.
b_bassa-afram.etymology_analysis: Hyphenated compound combining the Bassa traditional area name with the Afram River basin.

b_afram.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Afram River and Afram Plains are documented in modern geographical and historical sources.

morphemes.translation: Afram River and river deity Bosomafram

b_afram.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Akan hydronym for the 100 km tributary of the Volta River draining the Kwahu Plateau, also revered as the river deity Bosomafram.

b_wusuta.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Wusuta is an Ewe settlement in North Dayi District, Volta Region, Ghana, documented only in colonial and modern administrative records.

morphemes.translation: indigenous settlement name (etymology unattested in pre-modern written sources)

b_wusuta.etymology_analysis: Wusuta is an Ewe-speaking town in North Dayi District, Ghana; Ewe migration traditions place settlement in the Volta basin in the early modern period (post-Notsé exodus, c. 17th century).

b_amezdofe.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Avatime/Ewe mountain settlement in Ghana is documented in 19th-century missionary and colonial records (e.g., 1892 Basel/Bremen mission photographs).
b_amezdofe.etymology_analysis: From Ewe Amedzofe ('origin/home of humanity'), also used in Ewe oral tradition as a name for ancestral Ketu before the migration into Togo and Ghana.

b_lome.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; founded by Ewe settlers in the 18th–19th century (commonly dated to c. 1880) and documented in German colonial treaties from 1884 onward.

morphemes.translation: place of alo (a local shrub/tree) or market settlement

b_lome.etymology_analysis: Coastal Ewe settlement founded in the 18th–19th century that expanded rapidly as a trading port in the 1880s under German Togoland.

b_keta.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; settled by the Anlo Ewe and documented in European coastal trading records from the 17th century (Dutch presence from the 1640s).
b_keta.etymology_analysis: From Ewe ke ('sand') + ta ('head/top'), referring to the sandy spit between the Keta Lagoon and the Gulf of Guinea.

b_akpafu.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Akpafu (Siwu-speaking Guan/Togo Remnant community in Ghana's Oti Region) is documented only in colonial and modern ethnographic/administrative records.

morphemes.translation: traditional area and people name (endonym Mawu / Siwu)

b_akpafu.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Akpafu traditional area (oldest village Akpafu-Todzi, Siwu 'kaa i kato', 'home up high') in eastern Ghana.

b_nanumba.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Nanumba kingdom (Nanung, centered at Bimbilla) was founded c. 1200s–1300s according to oral tradition and documented only in later Arabic/colonial sources.
b_nanumba.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and polity name for the Nanumba people of Nanung in northern Ghana, traditionally founded by Naa Gmantambo (son of Naa Gbewaa) around the 13th–14th centuries.

b_kete-karachi.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Kete Krachi (twin settlement of indigenous Krachi and Muslim/Hausa trader quarter Kete) is documented in 19th-century trade and German colonial records.
b_kete-karachi.etymology_analysis: Compound of the trading quarter Kete and the Guan town Krachi (Krakye) on the Volta River, famous as the center of the Dente shrine.

b_bonduku.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; while Binger (1892) speculated a pre-1043 foundation, local chronicles and historians place Bondoukou's rise after Begho (c. 16th–17th century) under Dyula and Abron (Gyaman) rule.
b_bonduku.etymology_analysis: Major commercial and Islamic center in northeastern Côte d'Ivoire, associated with the Abron Kingdom of Gyaman (founded 17th century) and Dyula merchants from Begho.

b_bohi.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Bohi is a locality in Bondoukou Department, Zanzan District, Côte d'Ivoire, documented only in modern colonial/post-colonial censuses.
b_bohi.etymology_analysis: Small settlement in Appimandoum sub-prefecture, Bondoukou Department, northeastern Côte d'Ivoire; no pre-modern written attestation.

b_zanzan.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Zanzan is a modern administrative district (and 1997–2011 region) in northeastern Côte d'Ivoire centered on Bondoukou.

morphemes.translation: regional name in northeastern Côte d'Ivoire

b_zanzan.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym used for Zanzan District in northeastern Côte d'Ivoire; no written attestation prior to the modern era.

b_nassian.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Nassian (in Bounkani Region, Côte d'Ivoire) was first documented in late 19th-century European exploration accounts (Bowdich, Binger).
b_nassian.etymology_analysis: Koulango-speaking town in northeastern Côte d'Ivoire, seat of Nassian Department; no pre-19th-century written attestation.

b_ndenye.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Anyi kingdom of Indénié (Ndenye) was established in the mid-17th to early 18th century by Akan migrants from present-day Ghana.
b_ndenye.etymology_analysis: Polity and subgroup name of the Anyi-Ndenye (Indénié) centered around Abengourou in eastern Côte d'Ivoire, formed during the 17th–18th century Akan migrations.

b_diabe.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Agni-Diabè (Diabè) are an Anyi subgroup in eastern Côte d'Ivoire formed after 17th–18th century Akan migrations.
b_diabe.etymology_analysis: Name of the Agni-Diabè subgroup and traditional territory in eastern Côte d'Ivoire (around Agnibilékrou/Abengourou); no pre-modern written attestation.

b_satama-sokoro.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Satama-Sokoro (in Dabakala Department, Côte d'Ivoire) is documented only in colonial and modern administrative records.
b_satama-sokoro.etymology_analysis: Compound toponym in north-central Côte d'Ivoire where Mande/Dyula sokoro means 'old town/village' (contrasted with Satama-Sokoura, 'new town').

b_busa.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; while oral tradition (Kisra legend) attributes its founding to Woru, Bussa enters dated European written records in 1806 when Mungo Park perished at the Bussa rapids.
b_busa.etymology_analysis: Historic capital of northern Borgu on the Niger River (submerged by Kainji Lake in 1968 and relocated to New Bussa); no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kaiama.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; oral and archival traditions place Kaiama's establishment from Nikki in the 17th century, with European accounts beginning in the early 19th century.
b_kaiama.etymology_analysis: Borgu town and emirate in Kwara State, Nigeria, established as an offshoot of Nikki in the 17th century.

b_moshi.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Moshi River (a tributary of the Niger in Borgu) is recorded in 1820 in Joseph Dupuis's Kumasi itineraries and in later colonial maps.

morphemes.translation: river name (tributary of the Niger in Borgu)

b_moshi.etymology_analysis: Hydronym referring to the Moshi River flowing through Borgu (between Kaiama and Oyo) into the Niger River.

b_djugu.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Djougou in northwestern Benin emerged as a caravan market town around the 16th century with Dendi trader migration.
b_djugu.etymology_analysis: Major market city in northwestern Benin (Donga Department), historically a Dendi/Yom trading hub on the caravan routes.

b_parakou.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Parakou (capital of the Kobourou Bariba kingdom) is traditionally dated to around the 16th century and documented in 19th-century caravan records.
b_parakou.etymology_analysis: Seat of the Bariba Kobourou kingdom in northern Benin, founded as a trading crossroads on trans-regional caravan routes.

b_ilesa.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Ilesha Baruba (in Baruten LGA, Kwara State, Nigeria) is documented only in 19th-century Borgu route records and colonial administration.
b_ilesa.etymology_analysis: Borgu emirate town in Baruten LGA, Kwara State, Nigeria, located along the Sokoto–Badagry caravan route.

b_okuta.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Okuta (in Baruten LGA, Kwara State, Nigeria) is documented only in colonial and modern Nigerian records.
b_okuta.etymology_analysis: Town in Baruten LGA, Kwara State, Nigeria; the name corresponds to Yoruba òkúta ('stone/rock', a generic noun, not a proper natural feature name).

b_kenu.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Kenu is a ward/town in Baruten LGA, Kwara State, Nigeria, documented only in modern administrative records.
b_kenu.etymology_analysis: Baatonum-speaking settlement in Baruten LGA, Kwara State, Nigeria; no pre-modern written attestation.

b_ilo.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Illo was one of the Northern Borgu Kingdoms (traditionally linked to Kisra's son), documented in 19th-century Sokoto/Gwandu and 1898 Anglo-French pact archives.

morphemes.translation: northern Borgu town and kingdom name

b_ilo.etymology_analysis: Historic northern Borgu town in Kebbi State, Nigeria, formerly under Bussa before being ceded to Sokoto/Gwandu in the 1898 Anglo-French pact.

b_madekali.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; archaeological excavations at Madekali (south of Malanville, Benin) show medieval mound deposits and post-13th-century occupation, but no <= 867 CE written record exists.
b_madekali.etymology_analysis: Town in northern Benin (south of Malanville) built on a medieval settlement mound (birni); archaeological dates are excluded from first_mention_year.

b_kaoje.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Kaoje (in Bagudo LGA, Kebbi State, Nigeria) is documented only in modern colonial and Nigerian administrative records.
b_kaoje.etymology_analysis: Town in Bagudo LGA, Kebbi State, Nigeria, near the Niger River and Borgu borderlands; no pre-modern written attestation.

b_nikki.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Nikki was founded as the principal Wasangari/Bariba kingdom of Borgu (traditionally linked to Kisra's son Sabi, c. 14th–15th century) and documented in 19th-century European/Arabic sources.
b_nikki.etymology_analysis: Historic capital of the Kingdom of Nikki in northeastern Benin, central seat of the Wasangari aristocracy and the annual Gaani festival.

b_kandi.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Kandi (a Bariba/Dendi market town in Alibori Department, Benin) is documented only in post-16th-century oral traditions and 19th-century colonial records.

morphemes.translation: market town and Bariba chiefdom name

b_kandi.etymology_analysis: Capital of Alibori Department in northeastern Benin, historically a Bariba Saka chiefdom and market town.

b_segbana.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Ségbana (in Alibori Department, Benin, near the Nigerian border) is documented only in modern colonial and post-colonial records.
b_segbana.etymology_analysis: Town and commune in Alibori Department, northeastern Benin, inhabited by Boko and Baatombu communities.

b_borgu.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Borgu (Bariba/Batombu confederation across northwestern Nigeria and northern Benin) is first attested in post-1500 Songhai/Arabic chronicles and European accounts.

morphemes.translation: regional name for the Bariba/Wasangari lands

b_borgu.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym for the historic Borgu confederation (Bussa, Nikki, Illo, Kaiama) spanning modern Benin and Nigeria.

b_nikki_west.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; geographical subdivision of the Nikki region in Benin with no pre-modern written attestation.
b_nikki_west.etymology_analysis: Descriptive geographical barony key denoting the western hinterland of Nikki in northern Benin.

b_savalu.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Savalou in central Benin was founded as a Mahi kingdom between the late 15th and 18th centuries according to oral tradition.
b_savalu.etymology_analysis: Historic Mahi kingdom and town in Collines Department, Benin, founded on the earlier site of Tchébélou.

b_kpessi.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Kpessi (a Gbe-speaking canton and people in Togo's Plateaux Region) is documented only in modern ethnographic and colonial records.
b_kpessi.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and canton name in south-central Togo, speaking Kpessi (a Gbe language related to Ewe).

b_weme.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Ouémé (Weme) River in Benin is documented in European coastal and colonial records from the early modern period.
b_weme.etymology_analysis: Hydronym for the Ouémé (Weme) River, the longest river entirely within Benin, which also gives its name to Ouémé Department and the Weme-Gbe speakers.

b_shabe.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Yoruba kingdom of Sabe (Shabe / Ṣábẹ̀ẹ́) around Savè in Benin was established in the pre-colonial era (c. 16th–18th century) and documented in 19th-century records.
b_shabe.etymology_analysis: Name of the Yoruba subgroup and kingdom of Sabe (Shabe) centered on Savè in central Benin.

b_save.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Savè (capital of the Yoruba Kingdom of Savè in Benin) is documented in early modern Oyo/Yoruba traditions and 19th-century European accounts.
b_save.etymology_analysis: Town in Collines Department, Benin, seat of the Yoruba Kingdom of Savè (Ṣábẹ̀ẹ́).

b_odo-akaba.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Odo-Akaba is a village in Toui arrondissement, Ouèssè commune, Collines Department, Benin, documented only in modern records.
b_odo-akaba.etymology_analysis: Yoruba/Mahi settlement name in Ouèssè commune, Collines Department, Benin, combining Yoruba odò ('stream/river') with Akaba.

b_sokode.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Sokodé (chief town of the Tem/Kotokoli in central Togo) is documented in 19th-century caravan and German colonial records.
b_sokode.etymology_analysis: Second-largest city of Togo and capital of Centrale Region, traditionally derived from the Tem word for 'stone'.

b_kotokol.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Kotokoli (exonym for the Tem people of central Togo) is documented in 19th-century regional and colonial sources.
b_kotokol.etymology_analysis: Historical exonym for the Tem people of central Togo (around Sokodé and Bafilo).

b_upper_mono.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Mono River of Togo and Benin is documented only in early modern and colonial-era geography.
b_upper_mono.etymology_analysis: Geographical designation for the upper basin of the Mono River in central Togo.

b_todo.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Tado (formerly Ezame) is the ancestral Aja royal city in southeastern Togo whose kingdom flourished c. 15th–17th centuries.
b_todo.etymology_analysis: Historical village in southeastern Togo near the Mono River, seat of the Aja Kingdom of Tado; oral tradition records an earlier name Ezame, unattested in <= 867 CE written sources.

b_notse.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Ewe Kingdom of Notsé was founded around the 15th century, with its walls (Agbogbo) built in the 16th–17th centuries.
b_notse.etymology_analysis: Town in Plateaux Region, Togo, central seat of the 15th–18th century Kingdom of Notsé prior to the Ewe exodus.

b_atakpame.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Atakpamé (founded by Ana/Ifè Yoruba and local communities) enters dated historical records with the Battle of Atakpamé in 1764.
b_atakpame.etymology_analysis: Town in Plateaux Region, Togo, historically settled by Ifè (Ana) Yoruba migrants and known from the 1764 Battle of Atakpamé.

b_bassa.first_mention_attestation: No written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Bassa (Grand Bassa / Bassa Cove, Liberia) is documented in early modern European coastal records and the 1832 Americo-Liberian settlement.

morphemes.translation: Bassa people and coastal region of Liberia

b_bassa.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and coastal territory of the Bassa (Kru) people in west-central Liberia (modern Grand Bassa County).

b_gebba.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Gebba is not established in available written sources.
b_gebba.etymology_analysis: Gebba is a sub-barony toponym assigned to c_bassa in Liberia; no dated written attestation <= 867 CE or documented etymology is recorded.

b_man.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Man is not established in available written sources.
b_man.etymology_analysis: Man is a market town in western Ivory Coast in the Montagnes District (Dan/Yacouba territory); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_da.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Da is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Dan (ethnonym of the Mande-speaking Dan/Yacouba people)

b_da.etymology_analysis: Reflects the ethnonym of the Dan (Da) people of northwestern Ivory Coast and northeastern Liberia; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_tura.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Tura is not established in available written sources.
b_tura.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Tura (Toura) Southern Mande-speaking people of the Monts du Toura region in western Ivory Coast; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_nuon.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Nuon is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Nuon (indigenous name of the Cestos River)

b_nuon.etymology_analysis: Nuon (also Nipoué) is the indigenous hydronym for the upper/middle Cestos River forming the Liberia–Ivory Coast border; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_gbanshay.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Gbanshay is not established in available written sources.
b_gbanshay.etymology_analysis: Gbanshay is a third-order administrative locality in Bong County, Liberia; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_manon.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Mano is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Mano ethnic group of Liberia and Guinea

b_manon.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym of the Mano (Manon/Mah) Mande-speaking people of northeastern Liberia and Guinea; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_guerze.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Guerze is not established in available written sources.
b_guerze.etymology_analysis: Guerze (French: Guerzé) is the Guinean exonym for the Kpelle people of southern Guinea and Liberia; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_kokasu.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kokasu is not established in available written sources.
b_kokasu.etymology_analysis: Kokasu is a settlement/toponym in central Liberia (distinct from the county seat Gola/Gole); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_kondo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kondo is not established in available written sources.
b_kondo.etymology_analysis: Refers to the historical Kondo Confederation centered at Bopolu in northwestern Liberia (Gbarpolu County); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_folgue_karu.first_mention_attestation: Olfert Dapper (1668, Naukeurige Beschrijvinge der Afrikaensche Gewesten) records the allied peoples Folgia and Karou in coastal/interior Liberia.
b_folgue_karu.etymology_analysis: Compound of two historical Liberian polities/peoples, Folgia (Folgue) and Karou (Karu), first documented in Olfert Dapper's 1668 account; post-867.

b_kpelle.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kpelle is not established in available written sources.
b_kpelle.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Kpelle, the largest Mande-speaking ethnic group of Liberia (who migrated from the Sudanic savanna in the 15th–16th centuries); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_kono.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kono is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Kono people and region of eastern Sierra Leone

b_kono.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Kono people who migrated from Mali/Guinea to eastern Sierra Leone around the mid-16th century; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_kuniki.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kunike is not established in available written sources.
b_kuniki.etymology_analysis: Kunike (also Kuniki) is a Temne chiefdom in Tonkolili District, Sierra Leone, whose foundation is traced in oral traditions to 16th-century Kuranko hunters; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_kuramora.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kuramora is not established in available written sources.
b_kuramora.etymology_analysis: Sub-barony toponym in Kono, Sierra Leone; no dated written attestation <= 867 CE or documented etymology is recorded.

b_bolm.first_mention_attestation: Duarte Pacheco Pereira (1506–1508, Esmeraldo de Situ Orbis) describes the Bulom (Bullom) people on the Sierra Leone coast.
b_bolm.etymology_analysis: Bolm is an early variant of Bullom (Sherbro), the coastal Atlantic-speaking people of Sierra Leone documented by Portuguese chronicler Duarte Pacheco Pereira in 1506–1508; post-867.

b_boulom.first_mention_attestation: Duarte Pacheco Pereira (1506–1508, Esmeraldo de Situ Orbis) describes the Bulom (Bullom/Boulom) people of coastal Sierra Leone.
b_boulom.etymology_analysis: French-orthography variant of Bullom (Bulom), first attested in European sources by Duarte Pacheco Pereira (1506–1508); post-867.

b_zilm.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Zilm is not established in available written sources.
b_zilm.etymology_analysis: Sub-barony toponym in the Sherbro/Bullom region of Sierra Leone; no dated written attestation <= 867 CE or documented etymology is recorded.

b_boubo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Boubo is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Boubo River in southern Ivory Coast

b_boubo.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 130-km Boubo River flowing through southern Ivory Coast into the Atlantic via Tagba Lagoon; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_bandama-west.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Bandama-West is not established in available written sources.
b_bandama-west.etymology_analysis: Refers to the western basin of the Bandama River, the longest river in Ivory Coast; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_davo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Davo is not established in available written sources.
b_davo.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Davo River, a major eastern tributary of the Sassandra River in southwestern Ivory Coast; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_dibri.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Dibri is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Dibri locality in southern Ivory Coast

b_dibri.etymology_analysis: Toponym in the Kru coastal region of Ivory Coast; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_neyo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Neyo is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Neyo people and language near Sassandra

b_neyo.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and glottonym of the Kru-speaking Neyo people living near the mouth of the Sassandra River in Ivory Coast; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_east_kru.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for East Kru is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Kru ethnic group of Liberia and Ivory Coast

b_east_kru.etymology_analysis: Refers to the eastern Kru-speaking peoples and coast of Liberia and western Ivory Coast; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_west_kru.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for West Kru is not established in available written sources.
b_west_kru.etymology_analysis: Refers to the western reach of the Kru / Krao coast in southeastern Liberia; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_sassandra.first_mention_attestation: Portuguese navigators João de Santarém and Pedro de Escobar reached the river mouth in 1471 and named it Rio de Santo André (San Andrea), later corrupted to Sassandra.

morphemes.translation: Saint Andrew (1471 Portuguese name corrupted to Sassandra)

b_sassandra.etymology_analysis: Sassandra is a coastal port town founded by Portuguese navigators in 1471 as Santo André (San Andrea), whose name was later distorted into Sassandra; post-867.

b_gagnoa.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Gagnoa is not established in available written sources.
b_gagnoa.etymology_analysis: Gagnoa (from Bété Go-gnoa, traditionally glossed as 'inhabitants of the cheesemakers') is a major Bété city in west-central Ivory Coast; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_upper_lobo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Upper Lobo is not established in available written sources.
b_upper_lobo.etymology_analysis: Refers to the upper reach of the Lobo River basin in western Ivory Coast; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_lower_lobo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Lower Lobo is not established in available written sources.
b_lower_lobo.etymology_analysis: Refers to the lower confluence of the Lobo River with the Sassandra River in western Ivory Coast; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_nalu.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Nalu is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Nalu people of coastal Guinea and Guinea-Bissau

b_nalu.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Nalu people inhabiting the coastal littorals of Guinea (Boké/Rio Nuñez) and Guinea-Bissau prior to the 14th–15th century Mandinka arrival; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_bake.first_mention_attestation: French naval and colonial records document the takeover of the Boké area along the Rio Nuñez by 1849 (with late 18th-century slaver barracoons).

morphemes.translation: Boké port town on the Rio Nuñez

b_bake.etymology_analysis: Boké (in-game b_bake) is a port town on the Rio Nuñez in Lower Guinea; documented in European colonial records from the late 18th–19th century (French takeover 1849); post-867.

b_konkure.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Konkouré is not established in available written sources.
b_konkure.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the 303-km Konkouré River rising in the Fouta Djallon highlands and flowing to the Atlantic Ocean in Guinea; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_tombo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Tombo is not established in available written sources.
b_tombo.etymology_analysis: Tombo (Tumbu) is a coastal fishing town in Western Area Rural District, Sierra Leone; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_kamabai-sanda.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kamabai-Sanda is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Sanda chiefdom group in northern Sierra Leone

b_kamabai-sanda.etymology_analysis: Compound of Kamabai (a Limba town in Bombali District) and Sanda (a chiefdom name in northern Sierra Leone); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_bombali.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Bombali is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Bombali district and chiefdom in northern Sierra Leone

b_bombali.etymology_analysis: Toponym of Bombali District (and Bombali Shebora chiefdom) in northern Sierra Leone; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_tamiso.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Tamiso is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Tamiso locality in northern Sierra Leone

b_tamiso.etymology_analysis: Tamiso is a populated place in Northern/North West Province, Sierra Leone; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_bilima.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Bilima is not established in available written sources.
b_bilima.etymology_analysis: Sub-barony toponym in the Sierra Leone–Guinea coastal/inland borderland; no dated written attestation <= 867 CE or documented etymology is recorded.

b_gomba.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Gomba is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Gomba locality in Lower Guinea / Sierra Leone

b_gomba.etymology_analysis: Toponym in Lower Guinea / northern Sierra Leone (cf. Gomba Seydouya in Lower Guinea); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_benna.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Benna is not established in available written sources.
b_benna.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Benna Massif in Maritime Guinea near the Sierra Leone border; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_tonko.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Tonko is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Tonko Limba chiefdom in Kambia District

b_tonko.etymology_analysis: Refers to Tonko Limba Chiefdom in Kambia District, northwestern Sierra Leone; no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.

b_kaneya.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kaneya is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: local toponym in northern Sierra Leone / Guinea

b_kaneya.etymology_analysis: Sub-barony toponym in c_temne (Sierra Leone–Guinea borderland); no dated written attestation <= 867 CE or documented etymology is recorded.

b_odienne.first_mention_attestation: French explorer René Caillié visited and documented Odienné in 1827; town founding is credited to Vakaba Touré (1800–1858).
b_odienne.etymology_analysis: Odienné is a city in northwestern Ivory Coast founded in the early 19th century (credited to Vakaba Touré, 1800–1858) and first documented in European travel writing by René Caillié in 1827; post-867.

b_samatigila.first_mention_attestation: No dated pre-colonial written attestation <= 867 CE; local oral tradition places its founding before c. 1815 CE (recorded in Djiguiba Camara's 1955 Essai d'histoire locale; elevated to a full-exercise commune by Ivorian Law no. 78-07 in 1978).

eponym.details: Named after its founder N'golodjan Koné, nicknamed 'samatigui' ('master of the elephants') in Malinké, with the locative suffix '-la' ('at the home of the master of the elephants').

b_samatigila.etymology_analysis: Samatiguila derives from Malinké samatigui-la ('at the home of the master of the elephants'), referring to its founder N'golodjan Koné, a renowned hunter nicknamed samatigui; post-867.

b_sanafula.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; constituent holding of the Malinke polity of Kabasarana (formed c. 1848 CE) in northwestern Côte d'Ivoire / southeastern Guinea.
b_sanafula.etymology_analysis: Manding (Malinke/Dyula) settlement toponym in the Kabasarana region of northwestern Côte d'Ivoire and southeastern Guinea, formed with the Manding locative/settlement suffix -fula.

b_fwala-konyan.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Fouala (Fwala) is a town and sub-prefecture in Beyla Prefecture in the Konyan region of southeastern Guinea, first documented in the colonial/modern era.
b_fwala-konyan.etymology_analysis: Compound of the settlement name Fouala (Fwala, also recorded as Foukala) in Beyla Prefecture and the regional name Konyan, the Manding-settled plateau of southeastern Guinea.

b_barala.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Barala is a Manding settlement in the Konyan / northwestern Côte d'Ivoire borderland without pre-867 documentary records.
b_barala.etymology_analysis: Manding toponym combining a root bara with the locative postposition -la ('at, place of').

b_beyta.first_mention_attestation: Earliest dated written colonial record is the establishment of the French post at Beyla in 1893 CE; Konyan oral tradition places its Dyula founding in the early 13th century (c. 1200 CE).
b_beyta.etymology_analysis: In-game 'Beyta' represents Beyla, the main town of the Konyan plateau in southeastern Guinea, formed with the Manding locative suffix -la ('place of').

b_musadugu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; oral traditions date its founding to c. 14th–16th century CE, and it was first documented in writing by Benjamin Anderson in Narrative of a Journey to Musardu (1870).

eponym.details: Named after Zo Musa (Musa Kòma), the legendary founder of Moussadougou in Konyan oral tradition (c. 14th–16th century CE), combined with Manding -dugu ('village/town/land').

b_musadugu.etymology_analysis: Manding compound Musadugu (French Moussadougou / Moussadou, Liberian English Musardu) meaning 'town/land of Musa', after its traditional founder Zo Musa.

b_mau.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; the Mahou (Mau) region of northwestern Côte d'Ivoire was settled by Northern Mande (Mahouka) speakers from the 16th century onward.
b_mau.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym Mau (French Mahou), denoting the historical territory of the Mahouka Manding speakers around Touba in western Côte d'Ivoire.

b_bafinko.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Bafinko is a hydronymic/local name in the Bafing (Mahou) region of western Côte d'Ivoire.
b_bafinko.etymology_analysis: Manding hydronym related to the Bafing River (ba-fin 'black river') with the Manding stream/creek element -ko.

b_touba.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Touba in western Côte d'Ivoire was founded by the Fadiga clan in the 18th century CE and entered colonial records in the late 19th century (e.g. French post established 1898 CE).
b_touba.etymology_analysis: Named after Arabic Ṭūbā ('blessedness, felicity', also a tree of Paradise in Islamic tradition), a common West African Islamic settlement name.

b_karagawa.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; unattested in pre-867 written sources.
b_karagawa.etymology_analysis: Local West African toponym in the Mau (Bafing) area of western Côte d'Ivoire; no documented pre-867 etymology or written record.

b_macenta.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Macenta in Forested Guinea is inhabited by Loma (Toma) speakers who migrated into the region from the 15th century onward, and first appears in French colonial records from the 1890s.
b_macenta.etymology_analysis: Loma (Toma) settlement name in southeastern Guinea, ending in the Southwestern Mande locative/settlement suffix -ta.

b_toma_toro.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Toma (French/Guinean name for the Loma people) emerged in Forested Guinea and northern Liberia from the 15th century onward.
b_toma_toro.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym Toma (used in Guinea for the Loma people, Southwestern Mande speakers of the Macenta–Lofa borderlands).

b_buzye.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Buzi (Buzye) is an older Liberian/coastal designation for the Loma/Toma people, attested in early 20th-century Liberian records (e.g. 1906).
b_buzye.etymology_analysis: Historical exonym/variant Buzi (Buzye) used in Liberia for the Loma (Toma) people and their settlements (such as Buzi Quarters).

b_bisandugu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bissandugu (Bissandougou) rose to prominence in 1875–1878 CE as the capital of Samori Ture's Wassoulou Empire and was the site of the 1887 Treaty of Bissandugu.
b_bisandugu.etymology_analysis: Manding toponym Bisandugu (French Bissandougou), formed with the Manding settlement element -dugu ('village, town, land').

b_basando.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bassando is a historical Manding territory in Upper Guinea near Sankaran and Toron, known from oral traditions (17th-century civil wars) and modern ethnography.
b_basando.etymology_analysis: Historical Manding choronym (Bassando) denoting a savanna-border territory in Upper Guinea adjacent to Toron and Sankaran.

b_kuliya.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; unattested in pre-867 written sources.
b_kuliya.etymology_analysis: Manding settlement name in the Toron region of Upper Guinea; no documented pre-867 written attestation.

b_krawi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Krawi (Krao/Kru) is the ethnonym of a coastal Kru-speaking people of eastern Liberia and western Côte d'Ivoire, documented only from the European/Americo-Liberian contact era.
b_krawi.etymology_analysis: Derived from Krawi (Klao/Krao), an indigenous coastal ethnonym from which the broader linguistic and ethnic label 'Kru' was adapted by European writers.

b_grebo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Grebo (Glebo) of southeastern Liberia first had extensive documented contact with American colonists of the Maryland Colonization Society beginning in 1827 CE.
b_grebo.etymology_analysis: From Glebo (anglicized Grebo), the ethnonym of the Seaside Grebo people of southeastern Liberia around Cape Palmas.

b_putu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Putu (Pudu) is a Sapo/Krahn division and mountain range in Grand Gedeh County, southeastern Liberia, whose oral migrations are dated to the late 18th century CE.
b_putu.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Kru (Sapo) name Putu (Pudu), denoting a Sapo subgroup and the Putu Mountains/district in southeastern Liberia.

b_lower_grebo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern English-compound geographical descriptor referring to the lower/coastal Grebo territory in southeastern Liberia.
b_lower_grebo.etymology_analysis: Modern English geographical modifier 'Lower' combined with the Kru ethnonym Grebo (Glebo).

b_wenyon.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; unattested in pre-867 written sources.
b_wenyon.etymology_analysis: Kru-region name (Wenyon) in southeastern Liberia / western Côte d'Ivoire; no documented pre-867 written attestation.

b_tabu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tabou is a coastal town and department in southwestern Côte d'Ivoire (Krumen/Grebo territory), documented only in the colonial and modern periods.
b_tabu.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Krumen (Kru) coastal toponym in southwestern Côte d'Ivoire near the Cavally River mouth.

b_nzo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; N'Zoo (Nzo) in Lola Prefecture, southeastern Guinea, began as a satellite village of Doromou before the arrival of the French in the late 19th/early 20th century.
b_nzo.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Mande toponym (N'Zoo / Nzo) in the Mount Nimba borderland of southeastern Guinea.

b_daboya.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; although archaeological excavations at Daboya show Iron Age occupation, the settlement (earlier called Burugu by the Dagomba) is only documented from the post-867 Dagbon and Gonja eras (conquered by Gonja in the late 17th century CE).
b_daboya.etymology_analysis: Salt-trading town on the White Volta in northern Ghana, known as Burugu ('well') in Dagbani before coming under Gonja control as Daboya in the late 17th century.

b_leo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Léo is a Gurunsi (Nuna) town and capital of Sissili Province in southern Burkina Faso without pre-867 written records.
b_leo.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Nuni (Northern Grusi / Gurunsi) toponym in southern Burkina Faso near the Ghanaian border.

b_upper_mole.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; geographical designation for the upper basin of the Mole River in northern Ghana, which gave its name to Mole Game Reserve (1958) and Mole National Park (1971).
b_upper_mole.etymology_analysis: English directional modifier 'Upper' applied to the Mole River, a seasonal tributary of the White Volta in northern Ghana.

b_yendi.first_mention_attestation: Earliest contemporary written mention is in the Arabic chronicle Kitāb Ghanjā (1750s CE, naming Yāni/Yendi); Dagbamba oral tradition attributes its founding to Yaa Naa Nyaɣisi (c. 1420–1500 CE).

morphemes.translation: seat of the Yaa Naa (king of Dagbon)

b_yendi.etymology_analysis: From Dagbani Yani ('Seat of the Yaa Naa'), anglicized as Yendi, the traditional capital of the Kingdom of Dagbon in northern Ghana.

b_salaga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Salaga rose to prominence in the 18th and 19th centuries CE as the major kola and slave market linking Asante with Hausaland.

morphemes.translation: to get used to a place of abode

b_salaga.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Dagbani word salgi, meaning 'to get used to a place of abode'.

b_mawli.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mawli is a stream in the Savannah Region of northern Ghana without pre-867 written records.
b_mawli.etymology_analysis: Indigenous hydronym (Mawli) for a stream in the Savannah Region of northern Ghana.

b_buipe.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Buipe was an important political and religious center of the Gonja kingdom from the 16th century CE and was documented in the Kitāb Ghunja (written at Buipe in the mid-1700s).
b_buipe.etymology_analysis: From Gonja Gbipe (modern Buipe), traditionally explained from gbi ('heavy load') with the Gonja locative suffix -pe.

b_mole_south.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern English-compound geographical descriptor referring to the southern basin of the Mole River in northern Ghana.
b_mole_south.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Mole River hydronym in northern Ghana with the English directional modifier 'South'.

b_bole2.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bole was founded as a Wangara kola-trading center in the Gonja kingdom and appears in written/historical records from the early 19th century (1818 war with Asante; Bolewura seat moved there in 1868).
b_bole2.etymology_analysis: Trading town in northwestern Gonja (Savannah Region, Ghana) founded by Wangara merchants on the kola route between Manding and Hausaland.

b_kuisugu.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; unattested in pre-867 written sources.
b_kuisugu.etymology_analysis: Gur-region toponym in the Atakora–Mamprusi zone; no documented pre-867 written attestation.

b_dikutateni.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; unattested in pre-867 written sources.
b_dikutateni.etymology_analysis: Gur (Atakora-region) settlement name; no documented pre-867 written attestation.

b_perma.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Perma is a town and arrondissement in the commune of Natitingou, Atakora Department, northwestern Benin, documented only in the modern era.
b_perma.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Gur toponym in the Atakora massif of northwestern Benin (commune of Natitingou).

b_bawku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Mamprusi accounts date their presence in Bawku to the 17th century CE, with the Bawku skin traditionally founded in 1721 CE.
b_bawku.etymology_analysis: Local Kusaal/Mampruli toponym in northeastern Ghana, variously glossed as 'valley' or 'place of wild sorghum'.

b_sansane_mango.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sansanné-Mango was founded c. 1764 CE when the Anufom (Chakosi) overthrew the Gurma village of Kondjoko and established their war camp; visited by Louis-Gustave Binger in August 1888.
b_sansane_mango.etymology_analysis: Compound of Hausa sansani ('war camp', spelled Sansanné in French) and Mango (the Manding name for Grumania/Gourma); known as N'Zara to Anufo speakers.

b_pusuga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; in Mole-Dagbani oral tradition, Naa Gbewaa settled and died at Pusiga in the 13th century CE, with no pre-867 written records.
b_pusuga.etymology_analysis: Gur (Kusaal/Mampruli) toponym in the Upper East Region of Ghana, famous as the traditional site of Naa Gbewaa's shrine.

b_jimbale.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Jimbale is a village in the North East / Northern Region of Ghana without pre-867 written records.
b_jimbale.etymology_analysis: Local Gur settlement name in northeastern Ghana (Bunkpurugu-Nakpanduri / East Mamprusi area).

b_sakogu.first_mention_attestation: No written or documentary attestation <= 867 CE; Sakogu is a town in East Mamprusi Municipal District, North East Region, Ghana, without pre-867 written records.
b_sakogu.etymology_analysis: Mampruli (Gur) settlement name in East Mamprusi, northern Ghana.

b_mekrou.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Mékrou River (a 410 km tributary of the Niger in Benin, Burkina Faso, and Niger) is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.
b_mekrou.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Mékrou River, rising near Kouandé in northern Benin and flowing northeast into the Niger River.

b_alibori.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Alibori River in northeastern Benin (which gave its name to Alibori Department in 1999) is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.
b_alibori.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Alibori River, a major right-bank tributary of the Niger River in northeastern Benin.

b_kouande.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kouandé in Atakora Department, Benin, is home to a Bariba constituent monarchy of the Borgu federation that has existed since at least the 18th century CE.
b_kouande.etymology_analysis: Bariba (Baatonum) toponym in northwestern Benin, seat of a historic Borgu kingdom.

b_yohongou.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Yohongou (Yahoungou) is a village in northwestern Benin where archaeological excavations of settlement mounds indicate Iron Age occupation around 1000 CE (post-867 and archaeological, not written).
b_yohongou.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Gur settlement name in northwestern Benin (Atakora region).

b_po.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Traditional foundation of Pô is placed around 1500 CE by Kassena/Gurunsi communities; no pre-867 documentary source exists.
b_po.etymology_analysis: Pô is a Kassena (Gurunsi) town in southern Burkina Faso (Nahouri Province), traditionally founded around 1500 CE.

b_gurunsi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. The Gurunsi (Grunshi) are a collection of Gur-speaking peoples in southern Burkina Faso and northern Ghana; external written records date from the 19th century (e.g., Zabarima/Djerma campaigns).
b_gurunsi.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym referring to related Gur-speaking peoples (such as Kassena, Nuna, Lyela); one folk etymology derives it from Zarma 'guru-si' ('iron does not penetrate').

b_nakanbe.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Nakanbé (Nakambé) is the indigenous Burkinabé name for the White Volta River; European cartography ('Volta') dates from the Portuguese/colonial era.
b_nakanbe.etymology_analysis: Indigenous hydronym for the White Volta River (French: Volta blanche), rising in northern Burkina Faso and flowing south into Ghana.

b_wagadugu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Oral tradition places its founding around 1050 CE by Soninke Wangara migrants from Wagadu (Ghana Empire), later conquered by the Mossi in the 14th century; French colonial records date to 1896.
b_wagadugu.etymology_analysis: Wagadugu means 'home/land of the Wagu' (the Soninke subgroup associated with Wagadu/Ghana); Ouagadougou is the Francophone spelling.

b_guilongu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Guiloungou is a modern village near Ziniaré in Plateau-Central Region, Burkina Faso, with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_guilongu.etymology_analysis: Mooré-region settlement toponym in Oubritenga Province (near Ziniaré), Burkina Faso, known for pottery and modern Catholic parish/school institutions.

b_kayao.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Kayao is a town and department capital in Bazèga Province, central Burkina Faso, with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_kayao.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Mossi-region town name in Bazèga Province, Burkina Faso; no pre-867 written attestation exists.

b_calabar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. In-game name is Ibibo (referring to the Ibibio people of southeastern Nigeria), while the barony key is b_calabar (Calabar, founded/settled by Efik migrants in the pre-colonial era and documented by Europeans from the 15th-17th centuries).
b_calabar.etymology_analysis: Audited per in-game name Ibibo (Ibibio people of Akwa Ibom/Cross River); the key b_calabar refers to the port of Calabar (Akwa Akpa), which also lacks any written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_chukwu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Chukwu is the supreme deity of Igbo Odinani religion, not a documented pre-867 settlement.
b_chukwu.etymology_analysis: Igbo theonym meaning 'the Great Spirit' or 'Great Chi' (chi + ukwu), used here as a barony holding name.

b_bende.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Bende is an Igbo town and LGA in Abia State, Nigeria; written records date from the colonial era (post-1900 Aro Confederacy defeat).
b_bende.etymology_analysis: Igbo settlement and LGA name in Abia State (one of the four regions forming the acronym 'Abia').

b_idoma.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. The Idoma people inhabit Benue State south of the Benue River; Wikipedia notes Idomaland remained largely unknown to outside written records until the 1920s.
b_idoma.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Idoma people of Benue State, Nigeria, traditionally linked to ancestor Iduh and migrations from Apa (Kwararafa).

b_abakaliki.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Abakaliki (Ebonyi State, Nigeria) is documented as a slave-trade center from the 17th century onwards.
b_abakaliki.etymology_analysis: Derived from 'Aba Nkaleke', the name of a community in Izzi land (Northeastern Igbo).

b_uburu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Uburu (in Ohaozara LGA, Ebonyi State) is known in oral history for its pre-colonial salt lakes, with no documentary attestation <= 867 CE.
b_uburu.etymology_analysis: Igbo town in Ohaozara LGA, Ebonyi State, Nigeria, historically famous for traditional brine salt extraction.

b_otukpo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Otukpo is the traditional and administrative capital of the Idoma people in Benue State, documented in the colonial era (e.g., 1932 Eastern rail line).
b_otukpo.etymology_analysis: Idoma town in Benue State, Nigeria, traditionally founded by Agabi, son of Iduh.

b_igala.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. The Igala Kingdom (capital Idah) is traditionally dated to the 13th-16th centuries (Abutu-Eje) and lacks written documentary sources <= 867 CE.
b_igala.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and kingdom name (Anẹ Igáláà); one scholarly etymology derives it from 'Iga-ala' (wall/defense + sheep), though the origin remains debated.

b_ibah.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Minor Nigerian holding name in the Igala region with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_ibah.etymology_analysis: Local Nigerian toponym used as a constituent holding of Igala in-game.

b_east_igala.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. 'East Igala' is a modern English directional compound (standardized in repo as Ôst-Igale) rather than an attested pre-867 settlement.
b_east_igala.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound ('East Igala') denoting the eastern portion of Igala territory.

b_igbo-ukwu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. While Igbo-Ukwu is famous for 9th-10th century bronze-casting archaeological sites, archaeology does not constitute a written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE.
b_igbo-ukwu.etymology_analysis: Igbo toponym meaning 'Great Igbo'; the town was historically associated with the Kingdom of Nri and 9th-10th century lost-wax bronze artifacts.

b_onitsha.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Onitsha (Onicha) is a historic Niger River port city; British palm-oil traders and Christian missionaries established a permanent station there in 1857 CE.
b_onitsha.etymology_analysis: Igbo port city on the eastern bank of the Niger River (endonym Onicha), anglicized as Onitsha.

b_nsukka.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Although the Nsukka plateau has ancient iron-smelting archaeological sites, no written/documentary attestation exists <= 867 CE.
b_nsukka.etymology_analysis: Igbo town in Enugu State, Nigeria; oral traditions link it to the northern Igboland plateau.

b_south_igbo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. 'South Igbo' is a modern English directional compound (standardized in repo as Sût-Igbô) rather than an attested pre-867 settlement.
b_south_igbo.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound ('South Igbo') denoting the southern portion of Igboland.

b_bonny.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. In-game name is Ijaw (Ijo people), while the barony key is b_bonny (Bonny / Okoloama / Ibani, documented by Portuguese traders from the late 15th century).
b_bonny.etymology_analysis: In-game name Ijaw refers to the Ijo people of the Niger Delta; b_bonny refers to Bonny (originally Okoloama, 'town of curlews', and Ibani/Ubani), anglicized by European traders.

b_okrika.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Okrika (Wakirike) was established as an Ijaw fishing settlement and became the capital of the Okrika Kingdom in the early 17th century.
b_okrika.etymology_analysis: Ijaw port town on Okrika Island in Rivers State, Nigeria, capital of the 17th-century Okrika Kingdom.

b_nembe.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Nembe (Nembe-Brass) is an Ijaw kingdom in Bayelsa State, Nigeria, documented in European coastal trade records from the 18th-19th centuries.
b_nembe.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Ijaw town and kingdom name in the Niger Delta (Bayelsa State, Nigeria).

b_guwari.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Gwari (Hausa/Fulani exonym for the Gbagyi/Gbari people of central Nigeria) has no pre-867 written attestation.
b_guwari.etymology_analysis: Gwari (in-game: Guwari) is the Hausa/colonial exonym for the Gbagyi (Gbari) people of central Nigeria (Abuja, Niger, and Kaduna states).

b_taruga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Taruga is a famous Nok-culture archaeological site (iron smelting dated to c. 600 BCE) 60 km southeast of Abuja, but has no written/documentary attestation <= 867 CE.
b_taruga.etymology_analysis: Modern name of an archaeological site in central Nigeria excavated by Bernard Fagg in the 1960s for Nok iron-smelting furnaces.

b_minna.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Minna (capital of Niger State, Nigeria) grew into a major town in the colonial railway era (1908-1911); Paleolithic archaeology in the area is not a written attestation.
b_minna.etymology_analysis: Indigenous toponym of the capital of Niger State, Nigeria, historically inhabited by Gbagyi, Nupe, and Hausa communities.

b_kyadya.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. The Kyadya (Kede) are a riverine Nupe subgroup on the middle Niger, documented in Nupe oral tradition (pre-Tsoede/15th-16th c.) and 19th-century historical records (e.g., Ganigan War 1881-1882).
b_kyadya.etymology_analysis: Nupe ethnonym/polity name for the canoe-using riverine Nupe subgroup along the Niger River.

b_lokoja.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Lokoja was founded in 1857 CE by British explorer William Balfour Baikie as a trading post at the Niger-Benue confluence.

morphemes.translation: market town on the hill (proposed etymology)

b_lokoja.etymology_analysis: Disputed etymology: Oworo Yoruba 'Ilu Oke Oja' ('market town on the hill'), Hausa 'Loko Ja' ('red corner'), or Nupe 'Patti Lukongi' ('hill of doves').

b_kakanda.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. The Kakanda (Akanda / Hyabe) are a Nupoid-speaking riverine group near the Niger-Benue confluence, documented in 19th-20th century colonial and linguistic records.
b_kakanda.etymology_analysis: Nupoid ethnolinguistic name (also called Akanda or Hyabe) spoken along the Niger River from Eggan to Muregi.

b_raba.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. In-game name is Nupe (Nupe Kingdom, traditionally founded by Tsoede in the 15th-16th century), while the barony key is b_raba (Raba/Rabba, capital of Nupe until 1857, documented by Richard Lander in 1830 CE).

morphemes.translation: former Nupe capital on the Niger

b_raba.etymology_analysis: Audited per in-game name Nupe (the Nupe people and kingdom of central Nigeria); b_raba refers to Raba (Rabba), the pre-1857 Nupe capital.

b_bida.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Bida became the capital of the Bida Emirate (successor to the Nupe Kingdom) in 1857 CE under Usman Zaki and Masaba.
b_bida.etymology_analysis: Nupe city in Niger State, Nigeria, serving as the headquarters of the Bida Emirate since 1857.

b_kulfo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Kulfo was a major Nupe commercial and dyeing center documented by Captain Hugh Clapperton and Richard Lander in 1826 CE.
b_kulfo.etymology_analysis: Historical Nupe commercial transit town in Niger State, Nigeria, noted in 19th-century European travelogues.

b_kutigi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Kutigi (Lavun LGA, Niger State) appears in Nupe dynastic history from 1759 CE (exile of Etsu Jibrilu) and in 19th-century textile/dyeing records.
b_kutigi.etymology_analysis: Nupe town in Lavun LGA, Niger State, historically inhabited by Kintsozhi, Ndachezhi, and Konu weavers.

b_gbajigbo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Gbajigbo is a Nupe settlement in Mokwa LGA, Niger State, Nigeria, with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_gbajigbo.etymology_analysis: Nupe town/village toponym in Mokwa LGA, Niger State, Nigeria.

b_umaisha.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Umaisha (Yimaha) in Toto LGA, Nasarawa State, is the traditional headquarters of the Opanda (Egbura) Kingdom, which emerged c. 18th century.
b_umaisha.etymology_analysis: Egbura town on the Benue River in Nasarawa State, Nigeria (endonym Yimaha), serving as the seat of the Ohimegye of Opanda-Umaisha.

b_lower_guara.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. 'Lower Guara' is a modern English directional descriptor (standardized in repo as Nider-Guara) referring to the lower course of the Gurara River.

morphemes.translation: Gurara River (from deities Gura and Rara)

b_lower_guara.etymology_analysis: English directional compound ('Lower Guara') derived from the Gurara River, a tributary of the Niger; local folklore links Gurara to two deities, Gura and Rara.
