b_opanda.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. The Opanda (Egbura/Ebira) Kingdom in central Nigeria is documented from c. 1700-1780 CE onwards (with Umaisha as its seat).
b_opanda.etymology_analysis: Pre-colonial Egbura kingdom in Nasarawa State; the repo's 'Abalihistat' is a disambiguated Germanized label, while the actual barony is b_opanda (Opanda).

b_nok.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Nok is a Ham village in Kaduna State, Nigeria, famous for the Iron Age Nok culture (c. 1500 BCE-500 CE) discovered in 1928/1943, but has no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_nok.etymology_analysis: Ham village in Jaba LGA, southern Kaduna State, Nigeria, that gave its name to the prehistoric Nok culture.

b_boron.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Boron is a town in Dikodougou Department, Poro Region, north-central Ivory Coast, with no pre-867 documentary record.
b_boron.etymology_analysis: Town and sub-prefecture in Poro Region, Savanes District, northern Ivory Coast.

b_boron-north.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. 'Boron-North' is a modern English directional compound derived from Boron, Ivory Coast.
b_boron-north.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound ('Boron-North') based on Boron in northern Ivory Coast.

b_kweni-east.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. 'Kweni-East' is a modern English directional compound (standardized in repo as Ôst-Kwêni) based on the Kweni (Guro) people of Ivory Coast.
b_kweni-east.etymology_analysis: Modern English directional compound ('Kweni-East') referring to the eastern Kweni (Guro) region in Ivory Coast.

b_kweni.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Kweni (Kwéndré) is the endonym of the Guro (Gouro) Southern Mande people of central Ivory Coast; written records date from the colonial era.
b_kweni.etymology_analysis: Actual barony b_kweni refers to the Kweni (Guro) people of Ivory Coast; the repo's 'Dankarankirchen' is a disambiguated Germanized label.

b_kong-north.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Kong (northeastern Ivory Coast) was founded by Dyula merchants migrating from the Mali Empire starting in the 14th century and became the capital of the Kong Empire under Seku Watara in 1710 CE.
b_kong-north.etymology_analysis: Historic commercial and Islamic scholarly city in northeastern Ivory Coast, settled by Senufo/Tyefo agriculturalists and Dyula merchants from the 14th century.

b_kong.first_mention_attestation: Earliest contemporary written mention is in the Arabic chronicle Kitāb Ghanjā (1750s CE) and later European accounts (Binger, 1888); oral/dynastic tradition dates Seku Watara's founding of the Kong Empire to 1710 CE.

morphemes.translation: Kong (traditional toponym of the chiefdom and city-state)

b_kong.etymology_analysis: Auditing the actual barony Kong (disambiguated in the repo as Wulemarct). Kong began as a Fallafala Senufo chiefdom and became a major Dyula commercial center from the 14th century onward, rising to prominence as the capital of the Kong Empire under Seku Watara in 1710 CE. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_dabakala.first_mention_attestation: Louis-Gustave Binger, Du Niger au golfe de Guinée (1892), documenting the Djimini and Malinké settlement of Dabakala.

morphemes.translation: handle / shaft (from 'n'be daba kala', 'I make the daba')

b_dabakala.etymology_analysis: Dabakala is traditionally derived from the Malinké phrase 'n'be daba kala' ('I make the daba [hoe]'), spoken by a local blacksmith. Oral tradition places Senufo settlement in the 13th century and Malinké arrival in the 18th century, with written documentation beginning in the late 19th century (Binger 1892). No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_gyimini.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Djimini is not established in available written sources.
b_gyimini.etymology_analysis: Gyimini (modern Djimini / Dyimini) refers to a southern Senufo ethnolinguistic subgroup and their territory in northeastern Côte d'Ivoire (centered around Dabakala). The Senufo subgroups diverged from the 14th century onward; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_senufo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Senufo is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Senufo (external designation for the Gur-speaking agricultural peoples)

b_senufo.etymology_analysis: Senufo is an external (Mande/Dyula-derived) ethnolinguistic designation for a Gur-speaking population spanning northern Côte d'Ivoire, southeastern Mali, and western Burkina Faso. Ethnogenesis and subgroup differentiation are dated to the 14th–16th centuries; no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_leraba.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Léraba is not established in available written sources.
b_leraba.etymology_analysis: The Léraba River forms part of the border between Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire and joins the Komoé River. It is an indigenous West African hydronym with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_upper_nzi.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Upper N'Zi is not established in available written sources.
b_upper_nzi.etymology_analysis: Auditing the in-game barony Upper Nzi (adapted in the repo as Ober-Nzi), representing the upper reach of the N'Zi River, a major left-bank tributary of the Bandama River in Côte d'Ivoire. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_korhogo.first_mention_attestation: Earliest contemporary written European account is Louis-Gustave Binger's 1888 expedition (Du Niger au Golfe de Guinée); Senufo/Dyula oral tradition places its founding around c. 1700 CE.
b_korhogo.etymology_analysis: Korhogo is a major Senufo city in northern Côte d'Ivoire whose name means 'heritage' in Senufo. Founded in the early 18th century by Nanguin (with oral traditions of 13th-century Senufo presence), it has no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_bouake.first_mention_attestation: French colonial records establishing a military post at Bouaké in 1899 CE (following its 19th-century founding as Gbèkèkro).

eponym.details: Named after 19th-century Baoulé leader Gossan Kwa Gbeke; originally Gbèkèkro ('settlement of Gbeke'), later adapted to Bouaké.

morphemes.translation: personal name of leader Gossan Kwa Gbeke

b_bouake.etymology_analysis: Auditing the actual barony Bouaké (rather than the county-seat fallback Nzî). Founded in the 1800s by Baoulé and Assabou migrants as Gbèkèkro ('town of Gbeke'), named after leader Gossan Kwa Gbeke, and established as a French post in 1899 CE. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_middle_nzi.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Middle N'Zi is not established in available written sources.
b_middle_nzi.etymology_analysis: Geographical subdivision representing the middle reach of the N'Zi River in central Côte d'Ivoire. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_eastern_nzi.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Eastern N'Zi is not established in available written sources.
b_eastern_nzi.etymology_analysis: Geographical subdivision representing the eastern basin of the N'Zi River in central Côte d'Ivoire. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_bandama.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Bandama is not established in available written sources.
b_bandama.etymology_analysis: The Bandama River is the longest river in Côte d'Ivoire (approx. 800 km), flowing south into the Tagba Lagoon. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_bobo_dyulasso.first_mention_attestation: Louis-Gustave Binger, Du Niger au Golfe de Guinée (1892), documenting his entry into Bobo-Dioulasso (traditionally founded as Sia in the 15th century).
b_bobo_dyulasso.etymology_analysis: Auditing the actual barony Bobo-Dioulasso (rather than the county-seat fallback Djulasô). In Dyula, Bɔbɔjulaso means 'home of the Bobo-Dioula'. According to local tradition, it was founded as Sia in the 15th century CE and conquered by Kong in the 1730s. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_buguriba.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Bougouriba is not established in available written sources.
b_buguriba.etymology_analysis: The Bougouriba River is a tributary of the Black Volta (Mouhoun) in southwestern Burkina Faso, also giving its name to Bougouriba Province. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_boromo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Boromo is not established in available written sources.
b_boromo.etymology_analysis: Auditing the actual barony Boromo (rather than the county-seat fallback Lobî). Boromo is a town and capital of Balé Province in Burkina Faso. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_lobi.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Lobi is not established in available written sources.
b_lobi.etymology_analysis: Auditing the actual barony Lobi (disambiguated in the repo as Sekkinstat). The Lobi are an ethnic group originating in present-day Ghana who migrated into southern Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire starting around 1770 CE. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_pura.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Poura is not established in available written sources.
b_pura.etymology_analysis: Poura (also Poura-Mine) is the capital of Poura Department in Balé Province, southern Burkina Faso, known for its gold deposits. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_kirikongo.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kirikongo is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Kirikongo (archaeological village site in the Mouhoun Bend)

b_kirikongo.etymology_analysis: Kirikongo is an archaeological site in the Mouhoun Bend region of Burkina Faso (excavated in 2004–2006, showing occupation c. 100–1700 CE). Archaeological dates do not constitute written documentary attestation, and no written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_loropeni.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Loropéni is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Loropéni (market town and fortified enclosure site)

b_loropeni.etymology_analysis: Loropéni is a market town in southern Burkina Faso near the UNESCO-listed stone Ruins of Loropéni (occupied by the Lohron/Kulango from at least the 11th century and prospering in the 14th–17th centuries). No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_iringu.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Iringou is not established in available written sources.
b_iringu.etymology_analysis: The Iringou River is a tributary of the Komoé River flowing through southern Burkina Faso and northeastern Côte d'Ivoire. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_komoe.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Komoé is not established in available written sources.
b_komoe.etymology_analysis: The Komoé (or Comoé) River originates on the Sikasso Plateau of Burkina Faso and flows ~700 km through Côte d'Ivoire into the Ébrié Lagoon. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_wa.first_mention_attestation: Late 19th-century colonial/demographic records estimating Wa's population at c. 8,000 in 1880 CE.

morphemes.translation: we came (from 'te wa kaa yeng seore', 'we came to watch a dance')

b_wa.etymology_analysis: Wa is the capital of the Upper West Region of Ghana. According to Dagbani etymology, Wa derives from 'te wa kaa yeng seore' ('we came to watch a dance'). No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_mouhoun.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Mouhoun is not established in available written sources.
b_mouhoun.etymology_analysis: Mouhoun is the indigenous name of the Black Volta River, which flows ~1,352 km through Burkina Faso and along the Ghana-Côte d'Ivoire border. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_bouna.first_mention_attestation: Earliest contemporary written mention is in the Arabic chronicle Kitāb Ghanjā (1750s CE, recording Buna/Bouna alongside Gonja and Kong); dynastic oral tradition places its founding in the late 16th–17th century.
b_bouna.etymology_analysis: Bouna (also Buna) in northeastern Côte d'Ivoire began as a Kulango and Dyula village before becoming a centralized kingdom in the late 16th century and a major center of Islamic learning. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_kulango.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Kulango is not established in available written sources.
b_kulango.etymology_analysis: Kulango (Koulango) refers to the Niger-Congo-speaking people and language group of northeastern Côte d'Ivoire and western Ghana. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_folona.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Folona is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Folona (historical region in southern Mali centered on Kadiolo)

b_folona.etymology_analysis: Auditing the actual barony Folona (rather than the county-seat fallback Njene). Folona is a historical region (kafo) in the Sikasso region of southern Mali with Kadiolo as its capital. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_bandama_springs.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Bandama Springs is not established in available written sources.
b_bandama_springs.etymology_analysis: Headwaters of the Bandama River in northern Côte d'Ivoire (between Korhogo and Boundiali). No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_upper_nyene.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Upper Nyene is not established in available written sources.
b_upper_nyene.etymology_analysis: Auditing the in-game barony Upper Nyene (adapted in the repo as Ober-Njene), representing the upper reach of the Nyene river basin in northern Côte d'Ivoire / southern Mali. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_lower_nyene.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Lower Nyene is not established in available written sources.
b_lower_nyene.etymology_analysis: Auditing the in-game barony Lower Nyene (adapted in the repo as Nider-Njene), representing the lower reach of the Nyene river basin. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_banifing.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Banifing is not established in available written sources.
b_banifing.etymology_analysis: Auditing the actual barony Banifing (rather than the county-seat fallback Tjendugû). The Banifing River is a major tributary of the Bagoé/Bani river system in southern Mali and Burkina Faso. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_baoule.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Baoulé is not established in available written sources.
b_baoule.etymology_analysis: The Baoulé River in Mali (distinct from the Akan Baoulé people of Côte d'Ivoire) derives from Manding meaning 'Red River' (contrasting with Bakoye 'White River' and Bafing 'Black River'). No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_degou.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Dégou is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Dégou (tributary in the Bani/Niger basin of Mali)

b_degou.etymology_analysis: The Dégou River is a river in the Bani/Niger drainage basin in southern Mali and northern Côte d'Ivoire. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_tudugu.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Tudugu is not established in available written sources.
b_tudugu.etymology_analysis: Tudugu (also Toudougou) is a Manding settlement/place name composed of tu ('forest, bush') + dugu ('village, land'). No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_worodugu.first_mention_attestation: Early 20th-century French colonial administrative records documenting Worodugu (such as the 1907 Worodugu exodus cases in Séguéla and Mankono).
b_worodugu.etymology_analysis: Worodougou (Worodugu) is a historical region and modern administrative region in northwestern Côte d'Ivoire. In Dyula/Malinké, worodugu literally means 'land of kola nuts' (and also denotes 'south'). No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_bou.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Bou is not established in available written sources.
b_bou.etymology_analysis: The Bou River is a right-bank tributary of the Bandama River in northern and central Côte d'Ivoire. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_seguela.first_mention_attestation: Early 20th-century French colonial records from Séguéla (e.g., 1905–1907 palaver records; orally founded by the Keita).
b_seguela.etymology_analysis: Séguéla is the seat of Worodougou Region and Woroba District in northwestern Côte d'Ivoire, traditionally founded by Keita migrants (descendants of Sundiata Keita, 13th century or later). No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_koro.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Koro is not established in available written sources.
b_koro.etymology_analysis: Koro is a town in Bafing Region, northwestern Côte d'Ivoire, whose name is locally derived from the korokoro-soun tree near which the settlement was established. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_worodugu_east.first_mention_attestation: No dated written attestation <= 867 CE; earliest documentary record for Eastern Worodougou is not established in available written sources.

morphemes.translation: Sundiata Keita (13th-century founder of the Mali Empire)

b_worodugu_east.etymology_analysis: In-game barony b_worodugu_east (eastern Worodougou), adapted in the repo as Soundiatasburch after Sundiata Keita (13th century). Neither Eastern Worodougou nor Soundiatasburch has any written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_tyeme.first_mention_attestation: René Caillié, Travels through Central Africa to Timbuctoo (1830), recording his five-month stay in 'Timé' beginning 3 August 1827 CE.
b_tyeme.etymology_analysis: Tiémé is a town in northwestern Côte d'Ivoire (Odienné Department), first documented in writing by French explorer René Caillié during his stay in 1827–1828 CE. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_benin-city.first_mention_attestation: Portuguese explorers under João Afonso de Aveiro reaching the Kingdom of Benin and its capital in c. 1485 CE, referring to the royal center as Benin.
b_benin-city.etymology_analysis: Benin City (Edo) was earlier known in oral tradition as Igodomigodo (c. 900–1180 CE), Ile-Ibinu (1180–1255 CE), and Ubini (1255–1440 CE), which Portuguese explorers rendered as 'Benin' upon contact in c. 1485 CE. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_benin.first_mention_attestation: Portuguese explorers under João Afonso de Aveiro reaching the Kingdom of Benin in c. 1485 CE.
b_benin.etymology_analysis: Auditing the actual barony Benin (disambiguated in the repo as Liutbrandstat). The Kingdom of Benin grew out of Igodomigodo around the 10th–11th century CE and was first documented in writing by Portuguese explorers in c. 1485 CE. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_benin_marshes.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Benin Marshes is a modern English geographic descriptor for the coastal wetlands and riverine marshes of the Kingdom of Benin (Benin itself is first attested in European sources in the late 15th century CE, e.g., 1485–1486 CE).

morphemes.translation: from Ubini / Ile-Ibinu, the Edo kingdom in southern Nigeria

b_benin_marshes.etymology_analysis: Modern English descriptive compound combining Benin (derived from Edo Ubini / Yoruba Ile-Ibinu) with the generic topographic term 'marshes', referring to the coastal swamp belt of Edo State and the Niger Delta fringe in southern Nigeria. Excluded from natural_proper_name as a locator/descriptive compound.

b_abomey.first_mention_attestation: Earliest contemporary written European accounts date to the 1720s–1730s (e.g., William Snelgrave, 1727/1734) following Dahomey's coastal expansion; Fon oral/dynastic chronology places the establishment of Abomey's royal palaces around c. 1625 CE.
b_abomey.etymology_analysis: Abomey (Fon: Agbomɛ) was founded in the early 17th century CE as the capital of the Kingdom of Dahomey on the Abomey plateau. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_whyidah.first_mention_attestation: Portuguese contact at Ouidah (Ajudá) in 1580 CE along the Slave Coast.

morphemes.translation: Xwéda (ethnic/kingdom name, anglicized as Whydah and gallicized as Ouidah)

b_whyidah.etymology_analysis: Whyidah (modern Ouidah / Whydah; locally Glexwe) takes its European name from the Xwéda (Hueda) people and Kingdom of Whydah, first reached by the Portuguese in 1580 CE. No written attestation exists <= 867 CE.

b_ibadan.first_mention_attestation: Founded as a Yoruba war camp in 1829 CE; earliest dated written European/missionary records begin with Church Missionary Society (CMS) missionaries David and Anna Hinderer arriving in 1853 CE.
b_ibadan.etymology_analysis: From Yoruba Ìbàdàn, contracted from Ẹ̀bá-Ọ̀dàn ('by the edge of the savanna/meadow'), describing its strategic position at the boundary between tropical forest and derived savanna.

b_ijaye.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Documented in 19th-century Yoruba Civil War and CMS missionary accounts (destroyed c. 1862–1863 CE during the Ijaye War with Ibadan and resettled as Orile Ijaye in 1895 CE).
b_ijaye.etymology_analysis: Yoruba settlement name (Ìjàyè, later Orile Ijaye 'original homestead of Ijaye'). No pre-867 documentary attestation exists.

b_abeokuta.first_mention_attestation: Founded c. 1830 CE by Egba refugees under Sodeke; documented in Church Missionary Society (CMS) records from 1845 CE onward and in accounts of the 1851 CE Battle of Abeokuta.
b_abeokuta.etymology_analysis: From Yoruba Abẹ́òkúta ('under the rock'), referring to the shelter provided by Olumo Rock to Egba refugees around 1830 CE. Uses generic topographic noun òkúta rather than the proper name Olumo.

b_ifonyin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Traditional Yoruba kingdom/community in southeastern Benin (Ifangni) and southwestern Ogun State, documented only in colonial-era and modern records.
b_ifonyin.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Ìfọ̀nyìn (French/Beninese orthography Ifangni), designating the historical Yoruba polity and town in the Plateau Department of Benin.

b_badagry.first_mention_attestation: Emerged as a coastal port after Huntokonu's 1736 CE trading post; attested in 18th-century European slave-trade accounts such as Archibald Dalzel's History of Dahomy (1793 CE, recording 1777 CE events).
b_badagry.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Gbe (Ogu/Gun) phrase Gbedeglime ('inside the blacksmith's walls'), locally Gbagli/Gbagle, anglicized as Badagry.

b_ilaro.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Founded in the 18th century CE by the Oyo warrior Aro and documented in 19th-century Yoruba war and British colonial records.

eponym.details: Named after Aro, an 18th-century warrior who migrated from Oyo and founded the town (Ìlú Àró, 'settlement of Aro').

b_ilaro.etymology_analysis: From Yoruba Ìlú Àró ('town/settlement of Aro'), contracted to Ìlaròó (Ilaro), after its 18th-century founder Aro.

b_ketu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Ancient Yoruba kingdom in modern Benin (Kétou); oral tradition attributes its founding to Ede, grandson of Oduduwa, and written records appear in 19th-century missionary and French colonial accounts (conquered by Dahomey in 1886 CE).
b_ketu.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Kétu (French Kétou). Earlier Gbe oral tradition refers to the area as Ketume ('in the sand') or Amedzorfe ('place of human origin'), without pre-867 written attestation.

b_ibarapa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Yoruba subgroup and territory in southwestern Oyo State documented in 19th–20th-century Yoruba histories (e.g., Samuel Johnson).
b_ibarapa.etymology_analysis: Yoruba ethnonym and regional toponym Ìbàràpá, traditionally derived from Egusi Ibara, a local melon cultivar extensively cultivated in the area.

b_ile-ife.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Although archaeological urbanism dates to c. 900–1400 CE and oral tradition places it as the Yoruba cradle, the earliest possible written allusion is the 16th-century Portuguese 'Ogane' (c. 1505–1552 CE) and direct 19th-century European/Yoruba accounts.
b_ile-ife.etymology_analysis: From Yoruba Ilé-Ifẹ̀ ('house/land of expansion'), the sacred spiritual and political center of the Yoruba.

b_ijesha.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Traditional polity centered at Ilesa (founded c. 1250–1300 CE); earliest European written account of Ilesa is by Rev. William Howard Clark in 1854 CE.
b_ijesha.etymology_analysis: From Yoruba Ìjẹ̀ṣà, traditionally explained as a contraction of Ìjẹ-òrìṣà ('food/feast of the orishas'), referring to their frequent deity festivals.

b_owo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Yoruba city-state flourishing c. 1400–1600 CE with 15th-century terracotta archaeology; documented only in later oral and colonial-era written histories.
b_owo.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Ọ̀wọ̀ (historically Ogho), meaning 'respect' or 'honor'. Currently unoccupied holding in repo.

b_ondo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Ondo Kingdom was traditionally founded c. 1510 CE by Pupupu; earliest dated written records appear in 1870–1875 CE British Lagos Colony and CMS missionary accounts.
b_ondo.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Oǹdó (also Ode Ondo), capital of the Ondo Kingdom established c. 1510 CE.

b_ijebu.first_mention_attestation: First attested in European writing by Duarte Pacheco Pereira in Esmeraldo de Situ Orbis (c. 1508 CE) as 'Geebu', a great city surrounded by a ditch ruled by 'Agusale' (Awujale).
b_ijebu.etymology_analysis: Yoruba ethnonym and toponym Ìjẹ̀bú, centered at Ijebu-Ode and famous for Sungbo's Eredo earthworks.

b_ikorodu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Traces its origins to the 17th century CE in oral tradition and appears in 19th-century Lagos colonial records.
b_ikorodu.etymology_analysis: From Yoruba Oko-Odú ('farm of the odú herb'), contracted to Ìkòròdú.

b_owu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Owu history is first documented around 1820 CE (Ago-Owu) and during the 1821–1826 CE Owu War against Ijebu and Ife.
b_owu.etymology_analysis: Yoruba kingdom and ethnonym Òwu (also Owu-Ipole / Orile-Owu).

b_oshun.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Named after the Osun River (and associated Yoruba river goddess Oshun), documented in 19th–20th-century ethnographic and geographical works.
b_oshun.etymology_analysis: Yoruba hydronym Ọ̀ṣun (anglicized Oshun/Osun), designating the major river in southwestern Nigeria and its tutelary orisha.

b_siluko.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Town in Ovia South-West LGA, Edo State, on the Siluko River, attested in colonial-era Benin ethnographic and administrative records.
b_siluko.etymology_analysis: Settlement name in western Edo State near the Siluko River, associated with pre-colonial Udo and Benin borderland traditions.

b_igana.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Yoruba town in Kajola LGA, Oyo State, documented in modern administrative and local historical records.
b_igana.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Ìgànná (anglicized Igana) in the Oke-Ogun region of Oyo State.

b_iseyin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Yoruba town in Oyo State documented in 19th-century Yoruba history and colonial records.
b_iseyin.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Ìsẹ́yìn, historically a major center of Aso-Oke weaving in the Oke-Ogun zone of Oyo State.

b_igbodo-saki.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Saki (Shaki) was part of the Oyo Empire and became a major Yoruba refugee center after 1835 CE, with an Anglican church established in the early 1860s CE.
b_igbodo-saki.etymology_analysis: Compound toponym pairing Igbodo with Ṣakí (Shaki), a historic town in northern Oyo State near the Ofiki River.

b_ajase_ipo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ajase Ipo (Ajasse Ipo), a historic Igbomina Yoruba town in Kwara State, Nigeria, is documented in 19th-century Ilorin/Yoruba war accounts and British colonial gazetteers (e.g., the 1918 CE Ilorin Provincial Gazetteer).

morphemes.translation: settlement name (place of victory or refuge)
Ipo subgroup/territory of the Igbomina Yoruba, seat of the Olupo

b_ajase_ipo.etymology_analysis: Yoruba settlement toponym (Àjàṣẹ́-Ìpó / Ajasse Ipo) in the Igbomina region of Kwara State, Nigeria, traditional seat of the Olupo and traced in oral tradition to migrations from Ile-Ife.

b_idofian.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Igbomina Yoruba town in Ifelodun LGA, Kwara State, documented in 19th–20th-century Ilorin/Igbomina records.
b_idofian.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Ìdòfìàn (Idofiyan) in Igbominaland, Kwara State; local tradition associates its founding with Odofin titleholders.

b_giragi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Village on the right bank of the Niger River known as a findspot of the Tsoede bronzes, first documented in scholarly publications between 1912 and 1933 CE.
b_giragi.etymology_analysis: Riverine settlement name in the Nupe-speaking Niger valley of Nigeria, associated with Tsoede bronze finds.

b_ilorin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Settled by the 18th century CE as an Oyo border town; first documented in European writing by Hugh Clapperton in 1826 CE and in 1820s Ilorin Emirate records.
b_ilorin.etymology_analysis: From Yoruba Ìlọrin, traditionally derived from òkúta ìlọ irin ('stone for sharpening iron'), or alternatively ìlú erin ('town of elephants').

b_tada.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Gbedegi/Nupe village on the Niger River famous for the Tada/Tsoede bronzes, first documented in publications between 1912 and 1933 CE.
b_tada.etymology_analysis: Nupe/Gbedegi riverine village name on the Niger River in Kwara State.

b_jebba.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Documented in 19th-century Niger River exploration and Yoruba/Nupe accounts.

eponym.details: Named after 19th-century warrior/chief Okedare Lanloke (nicknamed Ajebaba): local tradition derives Ijeba (anglicized Jebba) from 'ibi ti Lanloke Ajebaba ba si' ('where Lanloke Ajebaba settled').

b_jebba.etymology_analysis: Anglicization of Yoruba Ìjẹ̀bá, traditionally contracted from ibi ti Lanloke Ajebaba ba si ('where Lanloke Ajebaba settled'), replacing the earlier name Oogodo.

b_oyo-ile.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Capital of the Oyo Empire (earlier Diogun pottery archaeology is excluded); attested in European accounts as 'Eyeo' by William Snelgrave (1734 CE, with 1670s–1680s references) and visited by Hugh Clapperton in 1826 CE.
b_oyo-ile.etymology_analysis: From Yoruba Ọ̀yọ́-Ilé ('Old/Home Oyo'), distinguishing the ruined imperial capital from 19th-century New Oyo (Ọ̀yọ́ Àtìbà).

b_otefan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Known from 19th-century Yoruba oral and written accounts of the Battle of Otefan (c. 1830–1836 CE) between Oyo/Borgu and Ilorin/Sokoto.
b_otefan.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym associated with the early 19th-century Oyo-Ilorin wars.

b_ogbomoso.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Founded in the mid-17th century CE by Soun Ogunlola and documented in 19th-century Yoruba war and missionary accounts.
b_ogbomoso.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Ògbómọ̀ṣọ́, traditionally derived either from Ogunlola's phrase 'ẹ jẹ́ kí a máa ṣe òhún' ('let us manage that place') or 'Ogbori Elemoso' ('he who beheaded Elemoso').

b_oyo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Oyo ('Eyeo') is attested in European accounts by William Snelgrave (1734 CE, following 1670s–1680s references); New Oyo (Oyo Atiba) was founded in the 1830s CE.
b_oyo.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Ọ̀yọ́ (adapted in the repo's disambiguated church holding as 'Zant-Henrike').

b_igboho.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Founded in the 16th century CE by Alaafin Eguguojo as the temporary capital of the Oyo Empire (Oyo-Igboho).
b_igboho.etymology_analysis: Yoruba toponym Ìgbòho (Oyo-Igboho), fortified capital of the Oyo Empire during its 16th-century Nupe exile.

b_ikare.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ikare (Ikare-Akoko), a major Akoko Yoruba town in Ondo State, Nigeria, is documented in late 19th-century and British colonial-era administrative records.

morphemes.translation: Ikare (traditionally interpreted as a place of refuge or settlement)

b_ikare.etymology_analysis: Yoruba settlement toponym (Ìkàrẹ́ / Ikare-Akoko) in Ondo State, southwestern Nigeria, traditionally interpreted as a place of refuge/settlement founded by migrants from Ile-Ife under Owa Ale Agbaode.

b_ekiti.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Yoruba subgroup and upland region documented in 19th-century accounts of the Ekitiparapo (Kiriji) War (1877–1893 CE).
b_ekiti.etymology_analysis: From Yoruba Èkìtì, derived from òkìtì ('hill, mound'), referring to the rugged, hilly terrain of the region. Generic topographic noun rather than a proper natural name.

b_yagba.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Okun Yoruba subgroup and region in Kogi State, documented in 19th–20th-century colonial and ethnographic records.
b_yagba.etymology_analysis: Yoruba ethnonym and toponym Ìyàgbà (Yagba), an Okun Yoruba subgroup in Kogi State (adapted in the repo's disambiguated church holding as 'Zant-Folkhard').

b_edo.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. First attested in European written records following Portuguese contact: João Afonso de Aveiro visited Benin City (Edo) c. 1485 CE (following Rui de Sequeira's 1472 CE coastal voyage).
b_edo.etymology_analysis: Edo endonym Ẹ̀dó for Benin City and the Edo Kingdom (preceded in post-867 oral tradition by Igodomigodo, c. 900–1180 CE, and Ile-Ibinu, c. 1200 CE).

b_osse.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Named after the Osse River (Ovia River) flowing through Kogi, Ondo, and Edo States.
b_osse.etymology_analysis: Hydronym designating the Osse River (also known as the Ovia River) in southwestern Nigeria.

b_ode_itseriki.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Ancestral royal capital of the Itsekiri people and the Kingdom of Warri (founded c. 1480 CE by Olu Ginuwa; visited by Portuguese missionaries in the late 15th century CE).
b_ode_itseriki.etymology_analysis: From Itsekiri Òde-Ìtṣẹ́kírì ('town/settlement of the Itsekiri'), also known as Ale Iwere or Big Warri.
